title: Get a human on the line
summary: The words and buttons that most reliably escape an automated support agent.
changes: You are transferred to a person instead of looping through a menu or a chatbot.
steps: Say or type "agent", "representative", "operator" or "speak to a human". Repeat if it deflects.
On a phone menu, press 0 repeatedly. If that fails, press nothing at all — many systems transfer after two timeouts.
Say "complaint" or "cancel my account". Retention and complaints queues are almost always staffed by people.
In a chat window, type "human" three times in a row; many bots have an explicit escalation rule for this.
Failing all that, post publicly on the company's social media account. Those are monitored by people.
how: Most support systems have an escalation path, because regulators and refund costs require one. The trick is knowing the words that trigger it rather than the words the menu offers you.
caveats: Saying "cancel" may start an actual cancellation flow. Be ready to say you have changed your mind.
Some companies now have no human channel at all for free accounts. Written complaints and chargebacks are the remaining levers.

title: Read the news in the order it was published
summary: Subscribe to publications directly. No feed algorithm, no summary, no suggestions.
changes: You see every article from the sources you chose, newest first, and nothing else.
how: RSS is a plain list of a site's newest articles that almost every publication still produces, usually without advertising it. A reader collects them into one chronological list.
steps: Pick a reader. NetNewsWire is free with no account and syncs via iCloud.
Add sites by pasting their address; the reader usually finds the feed itself.
Most newspapers, blogs, YouTube channels and even some Reddit forums have feeds.
Check it once or twice a day rather than continuously; that is the real benefit.
caveats: Some publications provide headline-only feeds to drive clicks.
Feedly has added AI features; NetNewsWire and Miniflux have none at all.

title: News without a generated briefing on top
summary: Skip the aggregator's summary and go to the publications, or to a human-edited front page.
changes: You read headlines written by editors rather than a digest assembled by a model.

alternatives.label: Ground News — see the same story across outlets

how: Wire services and public broadcasters still run human-edited front pages. Ground News shows you how differently the same event is being reported, which no summary can do.
caveats: Google News offers no way to remove its generated briefings.
Ground News has a free tier; its most useful comparison features are paid.

title: Get the AI notetaker out of your meeting
summary: Remove the bot that joined uninvited, and stop yours from joining others.
changes: No transcript or summary is generated, and the silent participant leaves.
steps: In the meeting: open Participants, find the entry with "Notetaker", "AI Companion", "Otter" or similar, and remove it as you would any participant. Hosts can do this; you may need to ask the host.
Zoom: Settings → AI Companion → turn off meeting summary and smart recording. Account owners control it at zoom.us/profile/setting.
Google Meet: the host controls "Take notes for me"; ask them to turn it off. Recording and transcription are separate switches.
Teams: remove Copilot and any notetaker app from the meeting; your administrator controls whether it can be added at all.
Say at the start that you object. In most jurisdictions recording a meeting requires notice, and in several it requires consent.
caveats: In a workplace, the administrator's policy may override your personal setting.
Third-party notetakers join as ordinary participants, so removing them works exactly like removing a person.
Consent law varies. Objecting out loud is both polite and, in some places, legally significant.

title: See a page as it was before
summary: Read the version of an article or recipe from before the site was rewritten.
changes: You get the original text, often shorter and better, without the additions made since.
how: The Internet Archive has been keeping copies of the web since 1996. Paste any address and choose a date before the change you dislike.
steps: Copy the address of the page.
Paste it into web.archive.org.
Pick a year from the calendar — 2018 to 2021 is usually a good span for recipes and how-to writing.
caveats: Not every page is archived, and interactive pages often do not work.
The archive is a charity. If you use it often, consider donating.

title: A recipe, without the life story or the generated blog
summary: Go straight to the ingredients and the method.
changes: You get a list and steps instead of nine hundred words and a chatbot.
how: Restricting the search to kitchens that test their recipes avoids the enormous quantity of generated recipe content now flooding search. Browser reader mode then strips the preamble.
steps: Search using the button above.
On the page, use your browser's Reader view — the icon in the address bar on iPhone and Firefox, or Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+R.
Most recipe sites also have a "Jump to recipe" link at the top.
caveats: Some of these sites are subscription-based.
A recipe with no photographs of the finished dish in the comments is one nobody has cooked.

title: Strip a page down to its words
summary: Reader mode removes advertisements, pop-ups, related-article machinery and most inserted widgets.
changes: The article appears as plain text on a plain background, in a typeface you choose.
steps: iPhone Safari: tap the page-settings icon at the left of the address bar, then "Show Reader". Hold it to set a site to always open this way.
Firefox: the page icon in the address bar, or Ctrl+Alt+R.
Chrome desktop: enable Reading Mode from the three-dot menu → More tools.
Android Chrome: it offers "Simplified view" automatically on long articles; enable it in Settings → Accessibility.
how: Reader mode reconstructs the page from its article text alone. Anything injected around the article — including most generated summaries and suggestion panels — is simply not carried over.
caveats: It fails on pages with unusual layouts, and on some paywalled articles.
Safari's "always use Reader" per-site setting is the most useful part and the least known.

title: Maps without the generated recommendations
summary: Turn off the personalised suggestions, or use a map that never had any.
changes: You get a map and directions. Nothing suggests restaurants or summarises reviews at you.
how: OpenStreetMap is built by volunteers surveying places themselves. Organic Maps uses that data in a phone app that works offline and has no advertising, accounts or recommendation engine.
caveats: Business opening hours and live traffic are much weaker than Google's.
Organic Maps is excellent for walking, cycling and travel abroad; less so for city driving.

title: A weather forecast, plainly stated
summary: Go to the meteorological office rather than an app that narrates the forecast at you.
changes: You get the official forecast, the charts, and the warnings, written by meteorologists.
how: Most consumer weather apps resell the same national model data with a layer of interpretation on top. Going to the source removes the layer and is usually more accurate for warnings.
caveats: Official sites are less pretty and occasionally slower on a phone. Add one to your home screen and it behaves like an app.
Yr, run by the Norwegian broadcaster and meteorological institute, covers the whole world and is free of advertising.

title: Translate without the commentary
summary: Get the translation itself, without an assistant offering to explain, rewrite or expand it.
changes: Text in, text out. The web version is quieter than the apps.

alternatives.label: Wiktionary, for a single word done properly

how: Machine translation has always been statistical; the objection is usually to the assistant layered on top of it. DeepL's translator page is still just two boxes, and Wiktionary gives you etymology, usage and register that no translator will.
caveats: All machine translation is a machine. If you want a human, a professional translator is the answer and there is no substitute for one in legal or medical matters.
Both services process your text on their servers. Do not paste anything confidential.

title: Learn from a person, not a summary
summary: Where to go when you want the subject explained by somebody who knows it.
changes: You get depth, disagreement and somebody to ask, instead of a confident paragraph.

action.label: Find it in a library
action.placeholder: A subject you want to understand

how: A public library card gives you free access to books, and usually to paid course platforms and newspaper archives as well. It remains the best-value institution in the world.
caveats: Library digital lending varies enormously by country and council.

title: Keep generated edits out of your photographs
service: Google Photos, Apple Photos, Samsung Gallery
summary: Turn off the automatic enhancements and know where the edit labels live.
changes: Your photographs stay as taken, and edited ones carry a visible note that they were altered.
steps: iPhone: turning off Apple Intelligence removes Clean Up from the Photos editor. Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri.
Google Photos: the Magic Editor and Best Take are opt-in per edit; edited images carry an "AI info" note in their details.
Samsung: Settings → Advanced features → Galaxy AI, and in Gallery turn off automatic suggestions. Samsung stamps generated edits with a watermark and metadata.
To check any photograph: open its information panel and look for an AI or edit note.
caveats: Computational photography — the processing every phone does when the shutter is pressed — cannot be turned off, and is not what this entry is about. Shooting in RAW comes closest.
Edit labels survive in the file's metadata but are lost if the image is screenshotted.
